notes: Landmark familial asbestos exposure appeal; Court of Appeal reverses Morland J on 1960-65 foreseeability.

enrichment.short_title: Maguire v Harland & Wolff: foreseeability of familial asbestos exposure
key_facts: Teresa Maguire developed mesothelioma from secondary exposure to asbestos dust brought home on her husband James's work clothes from Harland & Wolff's Liverpool shipyard between 1961 and 1965.
Morland J held Harland & Wolff liable for failing to foresee that Mrs Maguire was at risk from the amount and frequency of her exposure when washing and handling his contaminated clothing.
Mrs Maguire died shortly after trial; her husband continued the claim as personal representative.
Harland & Wolff conceded breach of duty to the employee Mr Maguire but disputed any duty owed to a non-employee family member in the early 1960s.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against High Court judgment finding Harland & Wolff liable for familial asbestos exposure causing mesothelioma.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Morland J's finding of liability set aside; respondent ordered to pay appellants' costs and return sums paid on account of damages.
enrichment.ratio: In 1960-1965 a diligent employer keeping up with occupational literature could not reasonably have foreseen that a wife laundering an asbestos worker's clothes faced a serious risk of asbestos-related disease; courts should not impose hindsight standards in scientifically developing fields.
legal_issues: Whether an employer owed a duty of care to a worker's spouse from secondary domestic exposure to asbestos dust
Whether such harm was reasonably foreseeable in 1961-1965 given contemporary medical and regulatory knowledge
Application of Caparo foreseeability principles to familial exposure claims
Whether employers must anticipate unusual or scientifically emerging risks
linked_authorities: Thompson v Smiths Shiprepairers (North Shields) Ltd [1984] QB 405
Fairchild v Glenhaven Funeral Services Ltd [2002] UKHL 22

confidence.notes: Detailed appellate analysis of contemporary medical literature and clear allowance of appeal.

notes: Permission granted on manual handling error of principle; late witness statement applications refused.

enrichment.short_title: Brazier v Dolphin Fairway: permission on pallet-lifting negligence
key_facts: Mr Brazier claimed damages for a hernia injury from lifting a 6-feet by 6-feet wooden pallet down from a 6-feet stack at his workplace.
Judge Stewart QC dismissed the claim for insufficient evidence of the pallet's weight and absence of expert engineering evidence on forces and strains.
The employer's system requiring workers to lift down such pallets from height was known and accepted at trial.
Mr Brazier applied in person for permission to appeal and also sought relief against his former solicitors' conduct of the case.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal interlocutory refusal of a negligence claim at trial.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted on the negligence issue; applications relating to solicitors' conduct refused; appeal listed for a two-judge court.
enrichment.ratio: Where a worker is required to lift down a large wooden pallet designed for fork-lift use from six feet, it is arguable without further expert evidence that the system of work placed him at foreseeable risk of injury and the judge may have erred in requiring detailed weight evidence.
legal_issues: Whether the trial judge applied the wrong principle by requiring expert evidence of pallet weight
Whether a known system of manual pallet handling was inherently unsafe
Whether late witness statement and medical confidentiality applications should succeed

confidence.notes: Short permission judgment with clear reasoning on arguable error of principle though merits remain for full appeal.

notes: Iranian asylum JR; IAT remittal quashed for misunderstanding dog-incident evidence and inadequate-reasons threshold.

enrichment.short_title: Ghanbarpar v SSHD: quashing IAT remittal in Iranian asylum case
key_facts: Iranian claimant Omid Ghanbarpar claimed asylum based on political opposition, detention, and a satirical incident placing a mullah's turban on a dog.
Adjudicator Brewer found the claimant credible and allowed asylum and Article 3 human rights appeals.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal remitted for inadequate credibility findings, treating as fundamental the implausibility that the claimant did not foresee offence from the dog incident.
The IAT misunderstood the evidence because the claimant expressly intended to insult the authorities and understood the likely consequences.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision remitting an asylum appeal for rehearing.
enrichment.outcome: Claim allowed; IAT determination quashed; mandatory order requiring the IAT to dismiss the Secretary of State's appeal; defendant ordered to pay claimant's costs.
enrichment.ratio: An IAT may not lightly put positive credibility findings at risk by remittal where the adjudicator heard oral evidence; remittal for inadequate reasons requires clearly deficient reasoning, and an IAT decision founded on a fundamental misunderstanding of the evidence must be quashed.
legal_issues: Standard for IAT interference with adjudicator credibility findings
Whether the IAT erred in treating the dog incident as implausible
Whether remittal was warranted for inadequacy of reasons
Appropriate remedy where the Secretary of State's appeal should have been dismissed
linked_authorities: Oleed v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] 1 INLR 179
P v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] EWCA Civ 1640
Indrakumar v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] EWCA Civ 1677

confidence.notes: Detailed judicial review with explicit quashing and mandatory relief clearly reasoned.

notes: Lightman J on section 42 Partnership Act 1890; proprietary share of assets governs post-dissolution profit account.

enrichment.short_title: Gill v Sandhu: section 42 share of partnership assets
key_facts: Partners Sandhu and Gill dissolved their residential care home partnership at Leigh-on-Sea when Gill excluded Sandhu in April 1999.
Gill continued the business alone without consent, generating revenue and capital profits including a £250,000 increase in property value.
Sandhu owed Gill a substantial loan for capital contributions, leaving net partnership assets insufficient to repay capital in full.
Gill contended Sandhu's entitlement under section 42 should reflect net asset value after debts rather than equal proprietary ownership.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Master Bowles on construction of section 42 Partnership Act 1890 entitlement to post-dissolution profits.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; outgoing partner entitled to half share of profits attributable to use of partnership assets, subject to fair return for continuing partner's services.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 42 Partnership Act 1890 'share of the partnership assets' means the outgoing partner's share in the proprietary ownership of assets at dissolution, not his share of net assets after payment of partnership liabilities; Taylor v Grier No 3 was wrongly decided.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'share of the partnership assets' in section 42
Whether net asset deficiency reduces entitlement to post-dissolution profits
Accountability of a continuing partner carrying on business without authority after dissolution
Interaction of sections 42 and 44 on winding up

confidence.notes: Comprehensive Chancery judgment on settled partnership law with clear dismissal of appeal.

notes: Committal appeal dismissed; extension of time refused where applicant absent and withheld medical evidence.

enrichment.short_title: Rosenfeld v MoD: refusal to extend time for committal appeal
key_facts: Mr Rosenfeld was committed to 28 days' imprisonment by Newman J for breach of court orders, with execution suspended for four months on terms.
He filed his appellant's notice more than four months later, challenging the committal on grounds of an unfair hearing in his absence.
He sought adjournment citing ill-health but redacted the diagnosis on his medical certificate and refused to disclose it to the court.
The Secretary of State indicated breach of suspension terms but left enforcement to its discretion.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to enlarge time for appeal against committal order, listed with the substantive appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Adjournment refused; extension of time refused; appeal dismissed as out of time.
enrichment.ratio: An applicant who delays more than four months to appeal a committal order and fails to show intelligible grounds or justify absence, including by withholding medical evidence without good reason, is not entitled to an enlargement of time.
legal_issues: Whether time to appeal a committal order should be extended
Whether adjournment was warranted on medical grounds
Effect of applicant's refusal to disclose redacted medical evidence
Whether a withdrawal application should leave an appeal in limbo

confidence.notes: Brief procedural disposal with clear sequential reasoning on adjournment, time extension and dismissal.

notes: Landlord and Tenant Act 1954 section 30(1)(g) appeal dismissed; landlord failed to prove own business occupation intention.

enrichment.short_title: Zafiris v Liu: section 30(1)(g) landlord occupation ground
key_facts: Tenants Mr and Mrs Zafiris sought renewal of a business tenancy of a fish and chip shop at 81 High Street, Beighton, Sheffield.
Landlord Mr Liu opposed renewal under section 30(1)(g), claiming intention to occupy for his own Chinese catering business with his wife.
The judge found Liu intended occupation but not for his own business; the Wonder Kitchen arrangement was his wife's business with Liu as landlord.
Liu had previously sought to let adjacent premises to the tenants and sold Wonder Kitchen before the hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from county court trial of preliminary issue on landlord's section 30(1)(g) opposition to new business tenancy.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; tenants held entitled to a new tenancy.
enrichment.ratio: A landlord opposing renewal under section 30(1)(g) must prove a firm settled intention to occupy for a business to be carried on by him; a husband-and-wife arrangement where the wife operates the business and the husband collects rent does not satisfy the statutory requirement even if described informally as a partnership.
legal_issues: Burden and standard of proof for section 30(1)(g) landlord occupation
Whether informal husband-wife catering arrangements amount to landlord's own business
Distinction between landlord occupation and spouse's separate business
Appellate deference to trial judge's evaluation of witness credibility
linked_authorities: Gregson v Cyril Lord Ltd [1963] 1 WLR 41
Betty's Cafés Ltd v Phillips Furnishing Stores Ltd [1959] AC 20

confidence.notes: Detailed landlord and tenant analysis with clear fact-sensitive dismissal of appeal.

notes: Education negligence appeal dismissed; education officers may owe duty of care without blanket immunity.

enrichment.short_title: Carty v Croydon: education officer duty of care for SEN pupils
key_facts: Leon Carty, who had significant learning, language and behavioural difficulties, sued Croydon LEA for failures in special educational provision from the 1980s through 1993.

After breakdown of placements at St Nicholas and prolonged attendance at Sir Cyril Burt School, the claimant alleged negligent failure to reassess and amend his statement of special educational needs.
Gibbs J dismissed the claim; the appeal challenged failures after St Nicholas and in keeping the claimant at Cyril Burt from 1991 to 1993.
Education officer Mr McCormack and chief educational psychologist Mr Edwards gave evidence supporting the authority's decisions as professionally acceptable.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against trial dismissal of negligence claim for inadequate special educational provision by a local education authority.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; court held education officers may owe a duty of care but no breach was established on the facts.
enrichment.ratio: Education officers performing statutory SEN functions are not immune from common law negligence where they assume responsibilities towards a child, but decisions on placement and reassessment are judged by Bolam standards and will rarely be negligent unless plainly wrong given the complexity of the field.
legal_issues: Whether education officers owe a common law duty of care to children with special educational needs
Whether failure to reassess or amend a statement after placement breakdown is actionable negligence
Application of Caparo and Bolam to public authority education decisions
Distinction between breach of statutory duty and negligence claims after Phelps
linked_authorities: Phelps v Hillingdon London Borough Council [2001] 2 AC 619
Barrett v Enfield London Borough Council [2001] 2 AC 550
X (minors) v Bedfordshire County Council [1995] 2 AC 633
Bolam v Friern Hospital Management Committee [1957] 1 WLR 582

confidence.notes: Substantial appellate judgment clarifying education officer liability with detailed fact-based dismissal.

notes: Street robbery sentence appeal dismissed; four-year term upheld for escalating drug-driven offending.

enrichment.short_title: R v Shannon: four-year sentence for street robbery upheld
key_facts: Shannon, a 23-year-old heroin and crack cocaine addict, robbed a lone woman at night, threatening to kill her and claiming to have a knife before stealing her handbag.
She used the victim's stolen bank card hours later to buy goods worth over £40.
She had 34 prior convictions for 67 offences, mostly dishonesty, with repeated breaches of probation and licence supervision.
Judge Smith sentenced her to four years for robbery and one year concurrent for obtaining by deception, taking eight further offences into account.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against sentence by leave of the single judge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; total four-year custodial sentence upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Where street robbery involves a convincing knife threat, an apparent accomplice and a persistent offender whose offending is escalating to fund drug addiction, a four-year sentence after guilty plea may fall within the appropriate bracket even without use of a weapon or physical injury.
legal_issues: Appropriate sentencing bracket for street robbery under Lobban and Sawyers
Effect of knife threats without actual weapon use
Relevance of extensive prior dishonesty and drug addiction
Whether custodial treatment offers the only realistic prospect of rehabilitation
linked_authorities: Attorney General's Reference Nos 4 and 7 of 2002 (R v Lobban and Sawyers) [2002] 2 Cr App R(S) 345

confidence.notes: Clear sentencing facts and explicit application of Lobban and Sawyers guidance.

notes: Unsafe dangerous driving conviction quashed; substituted careless driving with reduced penalty points.

enrichment.short_title: R v Jeshani: misdirection on causing death by dangerous driving
key_facts: Lorry driver Jeshani was convicted of causing death by dangerous driving after a prostitute who had entered his cab without invitation exited at a junction and was run over as he turned left with the nearside door open.
The appellant gave a consistent account that he drove off to escape her and misjudged the corner; eyewitnesses supported much of his evidence.
The trial judge misdirected the jury by watering down the section 2A requirement that driving fall far below the competent careful standard.
When the jury asked for written clarification the judge repeated the inaccurate direction rather than the later correct formulation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction for causing death by dangerous driving by leave of the single judge.
enrichment.outcome: Conviction quashed as unsafe; substituted conviction for careless driving; absolute discharge preserved; penalty points reduced from six to three.
enrichment.ratio: A conviction for causing death by dangerous driving is unsafe where the judge conflated the high section 2A threshold with careless driving and, when the jury sought clarification, repeated the defective direction instead of correctly separating the two constituents of dangerousness.
legal_issues: Proper direction on section 2A dangerous driving threshold
Distinction between dangerous and careless driving
Whether juries should receive written clarification when requested
Appropriate substitute conviction and sentence after quashing

confidence.notes: Detailed analysis of summing-up defects and clear substituted conviction with adjusted penalty.

notes: Planning JR partly succeeded; committee misdirected on prior refusals and Article 22 reasons inadequate.

enrichment.short_title: Chisnell v Richmond: planning permission quashed for misdirection

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (General Development Procedure) Order 1995

key_facts: Richmond upon Thames granted planning permission for extensions at 173 Whitton Road, Twickenham, adjacent to the claimants' home at number 171.
Two earlier applications by Mr Dillon had been refused mainly because extensions were tantamount to a separate residential unit, not on general neighbour amenity grounds alone.
The planning committee was advised it would be difficult to refuse on neighbour impact without a material change of circumstances and that new amenity grounds could not be introduced.
The grant notice failed to provide a proper Article 22 summary of reasons, referring only to the officer report and minutes.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of planning committee decision granting residential extensions.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; planning permission quashed; defendants ordered to pay claimants' costs to be assessed.
enrichment.ratio: Planning committees must be told that prior delegated refusals are material considerations informing but not fettering their judgment; requiring material change of circumstances to raise neighbour amenity objections is a misdirection, and Article 22 requires a genuine summary of reasons rather than a global reference to pre-committee documents.
legal_issues: How prior delegated refusals affect committee discretion on neighbour amenity objections
Whether the committee was misdirected that its judgment was fettered
Compliance with Article 22 summary of reasons requirement
Whether detriment to neighbours in earlier refusals covered physical amenity impacts
linked_authorities: Spackman v Secretary of State for the Environment [1977] 1 All ER 257
North Wiltshire District Council v Secretary of State for the Environment [1993] 3 PLR 113

confidence.notes: Detailed planning judicial review with clear quashing though some grounds were narrowed at hearing.
